qs.q: The portal of entry for varicella‑zoster virus is:
qs.e: VZV is inhaled and infects the respiratory epithelium first before spreading systemically. The other options are not the usual entry route.

qs.q: When is a person with varicella‑zoster virus most contagious?
o: One to two days prior to the rash onset
After all the skin lesions have crusted over
When the active lesions become intensely pruritic
At the precise time the rash first appears
qs.e: Infectivity peaks during the prodrome, 1‑2 days before lesions develop. Contagiousness declines after lesions crust over.

qs.q: Following primary infection with varicella-zoster virus, where does the virus become latent, leading to potential reactivation as herpes zoster?
o: Spinal and cranial nerve roots and ganglia
Microglial cells residing in basal structures
Glial cells located within the cerebral cortex
Endothelial cells lining brain capillary walls
qs.e: Varicella-zoster virus becomes latent in spinal and cranial nerve roots and ganglia after primary infection. Reactivation can manifest as herpes zoster accompanied by mild meningoencephalitis.

qs.q: Which laboratory test finding from a Tzanck smear of a vesicular skin lesion is characteristic of both Herpes Simplex Virus and Varicella-Zoster Virus infections?
o: Multinucleated giant cells with inclusion bodies
Atypical Downey cells with indented nuclei
qs.e: Both HSV and VZV produce multinucleated giant cells and 'ground glass' chromatin on a Tzanck smear. Owl's eye intranuclear inclusions are characteristic of cytomegalovirus histology.

qs.q: A pregnant woman in her first trimester is infected with Varicella-Zoster Virus. Which finding is a component of congenital varicella syndrome?
qs.e: Congenital varicella syndrome resulting from first-trimester VZV infection features skin lesions, limb hypoplasia, chorioretinitis, and CNS defects. Microcephaly and brain calcification are classical signs of congenital cytomegalovirus infection.
qs.s: Herpesviruses: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Tx: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is a complication of Varicella-Zoster Virus infection in adults that may be fatal?
qs.e: VZV can cause pneumonia in adults, which may be fatal. Burkitt's lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma are associated with EBV, and heterophil-negative mono is associated with CMV.

qs.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of acyclovir in the management of Herpes Simplex Virus and Varicella-Zoster Virus infections?
qs.e: Acyclovir acts by inhibiting viral DNA polymerase, thereby halting viral replication during active infection. It does not eliminate viral latency or prevent retrograde transport to ganglia.

qs.q: A pregnant woman in her first trimester is diagnosed with a primary Varicella-Zoster Virus infection. Her developing fetus is at risk of developing congenital varicella syndrome. What is a key clinical feature of this syndrome?
qs.e: Primary maternal VZV infection in the first trimester can cause congenital varicella syndrome, characterized by skin lesions, limb hypoplasia, chorioretinitis, and CNS defects. Limb hypoplasia and skin lesions are classic structural manifestations, unlike temporal lobe necrosis which is seen in HSV encephalitis.

es.q: Herpesviridae are significant human pathogens known for their ability to establish latency and cause recurrent disease. 1. Briefly describe the general characteristics of all Herpesviruses. (3 marks) 2. Compare and contrast the pathogenesis, typical clinical presentations, and common latency sites f

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Varicella‑zoster virus (VZV) is a DNA poxvirus that causes primary varicella (chickenpox) and re‑activation zoster (shingles). It spreads via respiratory droplets and skin lesions, and latency resides in dorsal‑root ganglia.

sections.p: VZV is a large, enveloped double‑stranded DNA virus in the Herpesviridae family. After primary infection it establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia, reactivating when cell‑mediated immunity wanes.
b: Latency in dorsal‑root and cranial ganglia

sections.p: The virion contains a core with linear DNA, surrounded by a proteinaceous tegument and a lipid envelope studded with glycoproteins that mediate entry into respiratory epithelium.
b: Glycoprotein E (gE) essential for cell‑to‑cell spread

sections.p: Inhalation of aerosolised droplets or contact with vesicular fluid spreads VZV. After replication in the nasopharynx, it disseminates via bloodstream to skin. Latency follows neuronal transport to ganglia.

t.b: Is the rash caused by VZV? Positive PCR confirms VZV DNA, especially when clinical picture is atypical.
Has the patient had prior exposure? IgM indicates recent infection; IgG shows past infection or vaccination.

sections.p: Primary infection produces varicella (diffuse vesicular rash, fever). Reactivation yields herpes zoster, a painful, dermatomal vesicular eruption that can lead to post‑herpetic neuralgia.
b: Varicella: mild in children, severe in immunocompromised or adults
Zoster: risk ↑ with age >50, HIV, malignancy, steroids

sections.p: Clinical picture is usually sufficient, but laboratory confirmation is needed for atypical presentations, immunocompromised hosts, or when differentiating from HSV or drug eruptions.
b: Typical vesicular rash in successive crops

t.b: If unavailable, rely on clinical pattern and PCR when possible.
Does the sample contain VZV antigen? Positive DFA confirms VZV quickly.

sections.p: Antiviral therapy targets viral DNA polymerase. Early treatment (<72 h) reduces complications. Vaccination provides primary and booster immunity, crucial in low‑resource settings.
b: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir – inhibit viral DNA synthesis
Avoid steroids alone; they worsen viral replication
Varicella vaccine (live‑attenuated) for children; Shingles vaccine (recombinant) for adults >50

sections.p: Focus on the clinical timeline, latency, and risk factors for reactivation. Know how to differentiate varicella from measles, rubella, and HSV, and the indications for antiviral therapy.
b: Post‑herpetic neuralgia risk factors: age >60, severe acute pain

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading rash with fever in an immunocompromised adult
Zoster involving the eye (herpes zoster ophthalmicus)

faq.a: Yes; adults often have more severe disease and higher complication rates.

faq.q: Why does shingles cause pain before the rash appears?
faq.a: Viral replication in the sensory ganglion irritates nerves, producing prodromal neuropathic pain.

faq.q: Is the varicella vaccine safe in pregnancy?
faq.a: No; it is a live vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy.
